title: The 2026 M&A Report: How Non-AI Companies Win at AI Dealmaking
gist: BCG finds that capital markets reward nontech companies for buying AI software/application firms (0.8%+ announcement returns vs. near-zero for tech acquirers) but that the premium is speculative, not earned, pushing BCG to argue for a disciplined 'adopt/partner/build/buy' framework where ownership should be the exception, reserved for scarce assets that lock in a durable, data-driven edge.

themes.theme: Investors reward nontech AI buyers, but the reward is a bet, not proof

insights.claim: Nontech companies that acquire AI software and application companies earn average announcement returns of more than 0.8%, nearly three times the average return across all deals including non-AI ones, while the same type of acquisition by a technology company generates essentially no market reaction because investors treat it as table stakes.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Watch announcement-day stock reactions as a live signal: a nontech firm's AI acquisition is more likely to be read as a genuine strategic repositioning than the same deal done by a tech company, but that premium is an expectation, not validated value, so it raises the bar the acquirer must clear post-close.
insights.quote: Nontech buyers, by contrast, earn an average announcement return of more than 0.8%—nearly three times the average return across all deals (including non-AI deals).

insights.claim: Average announcement returns for AI-related acquisitions rise the further up the AI stack the target sits: roughly 0.3% for hardware and semiconductor deals, 0.4% for cloud and data-center targets, and 0.5% for AI software and application company acquisitions.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Deal premiums and market approval concentrate at the application layer, not in picks-and-shovels infrastructure, suggesting investors see more differentiated, defensible value the closer a target sits to the end customer.

themes.theme: AI dealmaking is moving up the stack and beyond M&A into alliances

insights.claim: AI acquisition activity surged in 2025 across every layer of the industry from hardware and infrastructure to software and applications, with dealmaking increasingly moving up the stack toward software and applications as AI models became more capable and adoption spread.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Expect deal flow to keep rotating from compute/infrastructure targets toward application-layer and data-layer targets as the AI buildout matures.
insights.locator: The Changing Shape of AI Dealmaking

insights.claim: Nontech companies, not technology companies, accounted for most acquisitions of AI software and application companies in 2025, an inversion of the buyer mix one might expect.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Cross-industry corporates, not Big Tech, are the marginal buyer of AI software assets today, which should widen the pool of potential acquirers and bidders that sellers and bankers target.
insights.locator: The Changing Shape of AI Dealmaking

insights.claim: The number of AI-related alliances more than doubled from 2024 to 2025, when companies formed more than 1,300 new arrangements, and these alliance structures now rival traditional M&A as a route to acquiring AI capabilities.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: M&A volume and pricing data alone understate the real scale of corporate AI activity; alliance and partnership counts are now a comparably important indicator of who is building real AI capability.
insights.locator: The Changing Shape of AI Dealmaking

insights.claim: A company should evaluate each AI capability along two dimensions, how strongly it can differentiate the business and how readily it can be sourced, which together produce a four-way choice: adopt when a capability is widely available and non-differentiating, partner when access is limited but ownership adds little value, build when the company can combine assets it already controls with widely available technology, and buy only when a strategically important advantage is locked inside a scarce external asset.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Use this matrix as a due-diligence filter before approving any AI acquisition: if the target's edge is replicable via partnership or internal build, paying a control premium is likely value-destructive.
insights.locator: Choosing the Right Approach: Adopt, Partner, Build, or Buy

insights.claim: For a non-AI company, genuine competitive differentiation rarely comes from the AI model itself, since models and tools are advancing so quickly they risk becoming outdated or commoditized; the durable edge instead resides in the proprietary data, workflows, intellectual property, or domain expertise that surround the model.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating an AI acquisition should ask whether the target's value sits in a fast-depreciating model or in hard-to-replicate proprietary data and workflows; only the latter justifies a control premium.

insights.claim: The guiding principle for securing AI capabilities is to use the lightest structure that provides the access or control needed to gain an advantage while preserving the freedom to switch as technology evolves, meaning winning companies should treat ownership as the exception and adaptability as the rule.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: This is a direct against-consensus signal for dealmakers defaulting to acquisitions: BCG's framework treats heavy M&A as a last resort rather than a first instinct in AI capability-building.
insights.quote: To meet investors’ expectations, winners will make ownership the exception and adaptability the rule.

themes.theme: Lighter deal structures carry underestimated execution risk

insights.claim: A BCG study found that roughly nine in ten partnerships between industrial and technology companies failed to meet their goals, and lighter structures such as partnerships carry their own risks including platform lock-in, disputes over intellectual property, and the possibility that a partner applies insights gained through the collaboration elsewhere in the sector.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: A partnership is not a low-risk alternative to M&A; it requires the same governance rigor, including clear data/IP ownership, portability and benchmarking rights, and an exit process, or it is likely to join the roughly 90% that fail.
insights.quote: roughly nine in ten partnerships between industrial and technology companies failed to meet their goals
insights.locator: Choosing the Right Approach: Adopt, Partner, Build, or Buy

insights.claim: Relatively few companies have converted AI adoption into measurable value, and the gap between leaders and laggards is strategic and operational rather than simply technological, meaning a company that cannot redesign its workflows will underperform regardless of whether it adopted, partnered, built, or bought its AI capability.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Investors should discount AI-capability announcements that aren't paired with evidence of workflow redesign; the deal structure choice is secondary to whether the organization can actually absorb and operationalize the capability.
insights.locator: Choosing the Right Approach: Adopt, Partner, Build, or Buy

themes.theme: Industrial and consumer sectors: buy for brand/product edge, partner for scale

insights.claim: Industrial companies pursue two main paths to AI, buying specialist firms when a capability provides a meaningful product edge and partnering with large technology platforms for underlying capabilities they don't need to build themselves, with the ultimate winners combining proprietary industry data and engineering expertise with large-scale AI infrastructure in a 'build' approach that neither pure software nor pure hardware competitors can match.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: In industrials, look for players pairing proprietary engineering/data assets with large AI-platform partnerships as the likely long-term winners over both software-only and hardware-only AI entrants.

insights.claim: Schneider Electric's 2026 agreement to acquire Cognite, a cloud-native industrial platform combining a unified data model with agentic AI capabilities, illustrates when outright ownership is warranted: Schneider plans to integrate Cognite into its wholly owned AVEVA business to control a data foundation it can embed across its portfolio, because the strategic value lies in controlling an increasingly important software-and-data layer of the product, not merely accessing AI.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: This is a concrete template for when 'buy' beats 'partner': when the target's data/software layer can be embedded portfolio-wide, ownership captures compounding value that a licensing or partnership arrangement would leave on the table.

insights.claim: Consumer goods companies buy AI capabilities when they strengthen something that distinguishes the brand, such as personalization, demand forecasting, and virtual try-on, but rely on large AI platforms plus smaller tools for broad productivity, marketing, product ideation, and creative testing, reflecting a broader shift from back-office efficiency toward placing AI at the heart of the customer experience.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: In consumer, the buy-vs-partner line tracks customer-facing differentiation: expect M&A concentrated in personalization/forecasting/try-on tech and partnerships for generic marketing and productivity tooling.

insights.claim: L'Oréal's 2025 collaboration with Nvidia, which gave it access to Nvidia's enterprise AI platform for 3D digital product rendering and marketing and was expanded into R&D in 2026 to accelerate formulation discovery, shows that L'Oréal's true source of advantage lies not in owning compute infrastructure or general-purpose AI frameworks but in its proprietary skin and hair biology data and the scientific expertise to interpret it.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: A template for 'partner' over 'buy': when the differentiator is proprietary domain data rather than the AI infrastructure itself, pairing external platform scale with in-house data is more capital-efficient than acquiring an AI infrastructure provider.

themes.theme: Energy: execution beats access, and oilfield services are flipping from AI buyer to AI seller

insights.claim: Energy companies rely more heavily on partnerships and minority investments than on large AI acquisitions because their highest-value AI applications, subsurface analysis, predictive maintenance, and grid optimization, are domains where the differentiator is execution rather than access to technology.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Don't expect large AI-driven M&A premiums in energy; capability access is being solved via cloud and specialist alliances, so value capture will show up in operating metrics, not deal headlines.

insights.claim: In 2025 the gap in lease operating expenses between top-quartile and bottom-quartile Permian shale operators exceeded $5 per barrel of oil equivalent, a spread attributable not to geology or asset vintage but to operational execution.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: For energy investors, operator-level operational execution (which AI can improve) is a bigger cost-per-barrel driver than which asset or geology a company holds, making execution quality a screenable differentiator among Permian operators.
insights.quote: the gap in lease operating expenses between top- and bottom-quartile Permian operators exceeded $5 per barrel of oil equivalent, a spread attributable not to geology or asset vintage, but to operational execution

insights.claim: Shell's collaboration with SparkCognition, announced in 2023 to apply generative AI to accelerate exploration and building on earlier well-pressure prediction work, aims to produce subsurface images using fewer seismic shots than conventional methods, with Shell contributing proprietary seismic data and subsurface expertise while SparkCognition supplies the AI, letting Shell gain the capability without buying and operating a software business.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: A clean template for 'partner over buy': complementary-asset alliances can deliver capability without balance-sheet commitment when neither party's proprietary asset (data vs. algorithm) is individually sufficient.

insights.claim: Oilfield services companies are evolving from technology buyers into technology sellers, packaging their industry expertise into AI software and even supplying AI computing infrastructure to other energy companies as growth in their traditional businesses slows; market coverage also frequently mislabels energy AI deals that are actually about powering data centers as if they were about deploying AI within energy company operations, which investors should distinguish.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jens-kengelbach
insights.so_what: Watch for oilfield services firms monetizing domain expertise as a new software/infrastructure revenue line as core growth slows, and screen 'AI-related' energy deal headlines carefully since many are power/data-center infrastructure plays rather than genuine operational-AI deployments.
